title: The Midterms Are Trump's Test — and India's Stakes Run Through Tariffs, Visas and Russian Oil
excerpt: Prediction markets give Democrats a 90% chance of taking the House on November 3. For India, a Democratic chamber would mean oversight hearings on tariffs and the H-1B fee rather than quick relief — leverage on money, not veto-proof lawmaking.
body:
• Democrats are heavy favourites for the House in the November 3 midterms: Kalshi traders price a 90% chance of a Democratic House and 62% for the Senate.
  • The Silver Bulletin generic-ballot average has Democrats ahead by 8.8 points; a CBS News/YouGov poll put President Trump's approval at 39%, with 29% approving on inflation.
  • For India, a Democratic House brings subpoena power and hearings on tariffs, the Graham Act duties on Russian-energy buyers and the $100,000 H-1B fee — but not veto-proof votes to overturn them.
  • All four Indian-American House members seeking re-election — Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam — are in races rated safe.

The November 3 midterms are, first, a referendum on President Donald Trump. They are also, as The Hindu's op-ed framing puts it, a test with India's stakes attached — because the policies a new Congress would scrutinize first are the ones that land hardest on India: tariffs, Russian-energy sanctions and skilled-worker visas.

The numbers behind the test

According to IANS, traders on the Kalshi prediction market gave Democrats a 90% chance of taking the House and a 62% chance of winning the Senate, with a 61% chance of a Democratic sweep of both chambers. The Silver Bulletin polling average had Democrats ahead by 8.8 points on the generic congressional ballot, and a CBS News/YouGov poll conducted September 30 to October 2 found 39% of Americans approving of Trump's job performance against 61% disapproving — and only 29% approving on inflation. The Senate remains the uncertain half: the Cook Political Report rates seven races as toss-ups, six of them Republican-held.

What a Democratic House can — and cannot — do for India

A Democratic House gains subpoena power and committee gavels, and House Democrats are preparing a broad oversight agenda. But London-based Chatham House cautions that the party's real leverage would be money, not foreign-policy law: Democrats would lack the votes to override presidential vetoes, and Trump's tariffs, imposed largely by executive action, could be challenged in hearings and forced votes without being overturned. The same logic applies to the Graham Act tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, which could take effect from October 18: the law requires the administration to justify such duties to Congress in writing at least 10 days in advance, a requirement a Democratic-led House would be well placed to press.

The visa file

The $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, which falls heavily on Indian professionals — historically the largest share of H-1B beneficiaries — is already in court: a federal judge in California blocked its enforcement on September 30 and the administration has appealed to the Ninth Circuit. A Democratic House could add hearings and spending riders to that legal fight. Any India-US trade agreement needing legislation would also face a more sceptical chamber.

The diaspora on the ballot

The current House has six Indian-American members. Raja Krishnamoorthi gave up his seat for a Senate run and lost the Illinois primary; Shri Thanedar lost his Michigan primary in August. The four seeking re-election, all Democrats, are in safe races. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot on November 3, with 218 seats needed for a House majority — and, for New Delhi, a result that changes the questions Washington asks about India more than the answers it can impose.
